entities.summary:
Prince Moriyoshi-shinnō (also known as Prince Morinaga, or Sonchō Hōshinnō as a monk) was a pivotal figure in 14th-century Japan, a son of Emperor Go-Daigo whose life epitomized the tumultuous transition from the Kamakura Shogunate to the Ashikaga Shogunate. Born in the late 13th century, his early life as a Buddhist monk at Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei did not prevent him from becoming a formidable military commander and a central leader of the imperial forces during the Kenmu Restoration. His unwavering loyalty to his father's vision of direct imperial rule, free from samurai dominance, positioned him as a direct ideological and military adversary to the rising power of Ashikaga Takauji.

Moriyoshi-shinnō's active involvement in the Kenmu Restoration began in 1331, when he renounced his monastic vows to raise armies in support of Emperor Go-Daigo's bid to overthrow the Kamakura Shogunate. He was instrumental in coordinating anti-shogunate forces across various provinces, earning him the prestigious title of Seii Taishōgun (Barbarian-Subduing Generalissimo) in 1333, a position traditionally held by the shoguns themselves. Despite his military successes, including significant victories against Hōjō clan forces, his political influence waned as Ashikaga Takauji's power grew within the restored imperial court. This internal rivalry culminated in his arrest in 1334, orchestrated by Takauji, who perceived the prince as a dangerous rival to his own ambitions.

entities.summary:
Prince Moriyoshi-shinnō (1308–1335), also known as Prince Morinaga, was a central figure in the Kenmu Restoration (1333–1336) in Japan, an audacious attempt to reassert direct imperial authority against the waning power of the Kamakura Shogunate. As the son of Emperor Go-Daigo, he embodied the complex intersection of imperial lineage, martial prowess, and Buddhist monasticism that characterized the tumultuous transition from the Kamakura to the Muromachi period. His brief but impactful life irrevocably shaped the early phases of the Northern and Southern Courts period, marking him as a pivotal, albeit tragic, hero for imperial loyalists.

Following his father's exile in 1331, Prince Moriyoshi, initially known as Prince Morinaga and serving as a *Tendai zaasu* (chief abbot) at Enryaku-ji, renounced his monastic vows to lead the imperial loyalist forces. He orchestrated a series of guerrilla campaigns and strategic alliances against the Hōjō clan, the de facto rulers under the Kamakura Shogunate, notably rallying support from provincial samurai and religious institutions. His strategic acumen contributed significantly to the overthrow of the Shogunate in 1333, a pivotal moment that briefly restored direct imperial rule under Emperor Go-Daigo. He was appointed *Seii Taishōgun* (Commander-in-Chief of the Expeditionary Force Against the Barbarians), a testament to his military leadership.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Moriyoshi-shinnō's military leadership was instrumental in the overthrow of the Kamakura Shogunate, fundamentally reshaping Japanese political landscape and directly contributing to the Kenmu Restoration. His subsequent execution by Ashikaga Takauji cleared the path for the establishment of the Ashikaga Shogunate and ignited the protracted Northern and Southern Courts period.
